title: The Quiet Radiators
premise: Paloma Nystrom has spent seven years tuning the radiators of the family house in Duluth, listening to its pipes the way others read diaries, while carefully never saying aloud what everyone knows: that their mother, Ingrid, a once-promising composer, did not write the songs she claimed to. When a late-night radio program broadcasts 'Winter Harbor'—a piece Ingrid swore was hers, written and never recorded—Paloma realizes someone else heard it first, and that the family's careful silence was built on a theft no one will name. As Ingrid's dementia accelerates and her sister Ruth arrives to manage the erasure, Paloma must decide whether protecting the mother means protecting the lie. The novel ends with Paloma playing the true melody back to Ingrid on the house's oldest radiator, an act of witness rather than accusation, and choosing to leave the house—and the silence—behind.
about_author: Jonah Underhill is the pen name of a former piano technician who spent a decade tuning instruments in the upper Midwest before turning to fiction. Their stories about inheritance and quiet complicity have appeared in several small literary journals.

chapters.title: The Tuning Fork
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A routine autumn visit to tune the house's radiators establishes their ritual of listening: each pipe holds a different room's history. They note, without alarm, that the downstairs radiator has gone flat—the one nearest where Mother's piano used to stand. Emotional beat: tender avoidance, love practiced as maintenance.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, with flashbacks. We learn the family arrangement: after Father's death, Paloma moved home ostensibly to help, actually to keep watch over what Ingrid might say. A scene at Sunday dinner shows the choreography of deflection when a cousin asks about Ingrid's composing years. Emotional beat: the exhaustion of vigilance.

chapters.title: Winter Harbor
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Insomniac, Paloma hears a late radio program play a haunting melody introduced as an unpublished work by a deceased composer named Elias Vann. Paloma knows every note—it is the song Ingrid hummed all through childhood, the one she called her own, never recorded. Emotional beat: vertigo; the floor of the family story gives way.

chapters.title: What the Pipes Remember
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma returns to the house and listens differently now, tracing how sound travels through the old steam system, reconstructing which rooms Ingrid practiced in, and when. The radiator near the sealed music room carries a distinctive rattle. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Ruth Comes with Boxes
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins with Aunt Ruth, who arrives to help 'transition' Ingrid into assisted living, bringing archival boxes she intends to curate. Ruth is brisk, loving, and controlling. Paloma watches her quietly remove sheet music from the shelves. Emotional beat: two kinds of protection colliding.

chapters.title: Ingrid, Bright and Slipping
chapters.summary: Ingrid's POV, fragmented and luminous. She moves between 1963 and the present, addressing her dead husband mid-sentence, playing phantom scales on the table. She asks Paloma if the radio man ever called back—a question that lands like a stone. Emotional beat: heartbreaking lucidity inside confusion.

chapters.title: The Question Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma finally voices it to Ruth: who wrote Winter Harbor? Ruth denies knowing any Vann, but her hands shake as she tapes a box shut. The sisters-in-law circle each other in the kitchen. Emotional beat: the family's founding silence cracking audibly.

chapters.title: Elias Vann, 1958–1991
chapters.summary: Research chapter, Paloma's POV. Library microfilm and a call to the radio station yield fragments: Vann was a composer who taught briefly in Duluth, died obscure, left notebooks to a former student. The student's name is redacted from the obituary. Emotional beat: obsession kindling; Paloma skipping work to dig.

chapters.title: The Music Room Is Sealed for a Reason
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma opens the locked music room against Ruth's explicit instruction. Dust, a gutted upright piano, and inside the bench, a pencil sketch of Winter Harbor dated 1959—in Vann's hand, annotated 'for I.' Emotional beat: awe curdling into betrayal; evidence is not the same as truth.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Sink
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Ruth then Paloma. Ruth catches Paloma with the sketch and finally tells her version: Ingrid and Vann were lovers; he gave her the song; after his death she let the world believe it was hers, and the family let her, because grief had already taken enough. Emotional beat: sympathy complicating outrage.

chapters.title: What Survival Cost
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, extended flashback to 1991–1992. Ruth, then young, helped bury the truth to shield Ingrid from scandal and ruin after Father's illness drained them. She argues that a stolen song was the price of a life. Emotional beat: Ruth's guilt reframed as sacrifice; the reader can no longer simply judge.

chapters.title: The Radio Man Calls Back
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The program producer contacts Paloma—Vann's estate is preparing a retrospective and wants testimony about regional performances. Someone mentioned a Duluth pianist who played Vann's work. Paloma lies badly on the phone, then sits in the dark realizing they've been given a deadline. Emotional beat: external pressure converting private doubt into public stakes.

chapters.title: Ingrid Sings It Wrong
chapters.summary: Ingrid's POV. Ingrid plays Winter Harbor from memory at the kitchen table, but her version drifts—she has altered it over decades until it is half hers. Paloma listens and understands something terrible and freeing: the song has genuinely become hybrid. Emotional beat: moral ground shifting underfoot.

chapters.title: The Notebooks Surface
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Tracking down Vann's former student leads to a storage unit in Superior containing his notebooks: pages showing Ingrid's own marginalia, her corrections, her additions—evidence she wasn't only a thief but a collaborator he acknowledged. Emotional beat: the binary of guilty/innocent collapsing.

chapters.title: Ruth Breaks Rank
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Pressured by the estate's lawyer and her own conscience, Ruth admits there are letters she never destroyed—letters from Vann to Ingrid that name their arrangement. She offers them to Paloma like a wound being opened. Emotional beat: surrender; the keeper of secrets choosing memory over mercy.

chapters.title: The Letters
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, reading interwoven with present scenes. The letters reveal a third possibility: Vann gave Ingrid the song deliberately, asking her to finish it because his hands were failing. She finished it and could never claim it without claiming him. Emotional beat: grief reorganizing everything Paloma thought they knew.

chapters.title: Assessment
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A doctor's evaluation confirms Ingrid's memory loss is accelerating; within a year she won't reliably know the song at all. Whatever must be asked or answered has a closing window. Ruth pushes to finalize the assisted-living transfer immediately. Emotional beat: urgency; time becoming antagonist.

chapters.title: The Arrangement Examined
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma confronts the real question—not whether Ingrid stole, but why the whole family arranged itself around never saying so, and what Paloma got out of seven years of almost saying it. A quiet scene alone in the sealed music room. Emotional beat: turning inward; complicity owned.

chapters.title: Playing It Back
chapters.summary: Climax, Paloma's POV. At the estate representative's visit, instead of testifying or denying, Paloma brings Ingrid to the old radiator, taps its pipes to reproduce Winter Harbor's true opening—the version from the 1959 sketch—and lets Ingrid hear her younger self in it. Ingrid, lucid for one moment, says: 'He asked me to make it mine.' Emotional beat: catharsis; witness without verdict.

chapters.title: What Gets Recorded
chapters.summary: Falling action, Paloma's POV. Paloma records Ingrid humming her hybrid version—one take, imperfect, trembling—and sends it to the estate with a letter explaining the collaboration, neither accusing nor absolving. Ruth reads the letter and, for the first time, doesn't correct it. Emotional beat: release; truth offered gently rather than wielded.

chapters.title: The House Lets Go
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Moving day. Ingrid settles into the care facility, humming the song as though it were a lullaby she invented this morning—which, in every way that matters now, she did. Paloma bleeds the radiators one last time and leaves the keys. Emotional beat: bittersweet departure; inheritance refused and transformed.

chapters.title: Coda: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Paloma's POV, months later. The retrospective airs; the program credits Winter Harbor to Elias Vann 'with significant realization by Ingrid Nystrom.' Paloma, tuning pianos in a new city, hears it from a stranger's open window and keeps walking. Emotional beat: quiet peace; the song survives truer than anyone who made it.
